'''''Scirpus''''' is a genus of grass-like species in the sedge family [[Cyperaceae]] many with the common names '''club-rush''', '''wood club-rush''' or '''bulrush'''. They mostly inhabit wetlands and damp locations.

==Description==
''Scirpus'' are rhizomatous perennial herbs, with 3-angled stems and flat grass-like leaves. The flowers are in clusters of small spikelets, often brown or greenish brown.<ref name="Stace">{{cite book|last=Stace|first=C. A.|author-link = Stace, C. A.|year=2019|title=New Flora of the British Isles|edition=Fourth|publisher=C & M Floristics|location=Middlewood Green, Suffolk, U.K.| isbn=978-1-5272-2630-2}}</ref>{{rp|992}} Some species (e.g. ''[[Schoenoplectus lacustris|S. lacustris]]'') can reach a height of {{Convert|3|m|abbr=off|frac=2}}, while ''[[Scirpus sylvaticus|S. sylvaticus]]'' is about {{Convert|1.2|m|ft|abbr=on|frac=2}} and others, such as ''[[Scirpus supinus|S. supinus]]'', are much smaller, only reaching {{Convert|20–30|cm|frac=2}} tall.

==Taxonomy==
The taxonomy of the genus is complex, and under review by [[botanists]]. Recent studies by [[Taxonomy (biology)|taxonomists]] of the Cyperaceae have resulted in the creation of several new genera, including the genera ''[[Schoenoplectus]]'' and ''[[Bolboschoenus]]''; others (including ''[[Blysmus]]'', ''[[Isolepis]]'', ''[[Nomochloa]]'', and ''[[Scirpoides]]'') have also been used. At one point this genus held almost 300 species, but many of the species once assigned to it have now been reassigned, and it now holds an estimated 120 species.

=== Fossil record ===
Several hundred [[fossil]] fruits of ''Scirpus ragozinii'' have been described from [[middle Miocene]] [[strata]] of the Fasterholt area near [[Silkeborg]] in Central [[Jutland]], [[Denmark]].<ref>Angiosperm Fruits and Seeds from the Middle Miocene of Jutland (Denmark) by Else Marie Friis, The Royal Danish Academy of Sciences and Letters 24:3, 1985</ref> Thirty-five [[fossil]] fruits of the extant ''Scirpus sylvaticus'' have been extracted from [[borehole]] samples of the [[Middle Miocene]] fresh water deposits in [[Nowy Sacz]] Basin, [[West Carpathians]], [[Poland]].<ref>Łańcucka-Środoniowa M.: Macroscopic plant remains from the freshwater Miocene of the Nowy Sącz Basin (West Carpathians, Poland) [Szczątki makroskopowe roślin z miocenu słodkowodnego Kotliny Sądeckiej (Karpaty Zachodnie, Polska)]. Acta Palaeobotanica 1979 20 (1): 3-117.</ref>

== Distribution and habitat ==
The genus has a nearly [[cosmopolitan distribution]], found on every continent except [[Africa]] and [[Antarctica]].<ref name="WCSP">{{cite web |url=http://apps.kew.org/wcsp/namedetail.do?name_id=263650 |title=Kew World Checklist of Selected Plant Families |publisher=Royal Botanic Garden Kew |access-date=9 December 2019 }}</ref>

Many species are common in [[wetlands]] and can produce dense stands of vegetation, along rivers,<ref name="Auclair">{{cite journal |author=Auclair, A. N. D. |author2=Bouchard, A. |author3=Pajaczkowski, J. |date=1976 |title=Plant standing crop and productivity relations in a Scirpus–Equisetum wetland |journal=Ecology |volume=57 |issue=5 |pages=941–52 |doi=10.2307/1941059 |jstor=1941059|bibcode=1976Ecol...57..941A }}</ref><ref name="Day">{{cite journal |author=Day, R. T. |author2=Keddy, P. A. |author3=McNeill, J. |author4=Carleton, T. |date=1988 |title=Fertility and disturbance gradients: a summary model for riverine marsh vegetation |journal=Ecology |volume=69 |issue=4 |pages=1044–54 |doi=10.2307/1941260 |jstor=1941260|bibcode=1988Ecol...69.1044D }}</ref> in coastal deltas<ref name="Gough">{{cite journal |author=Gough, L. G. |author2=Grace, J. B. |author3=Taylor, K. L. |date=1994 |title=The relationship between species richness and community biomass: the importance of environmental variables |journal=Oikos |volume=70 |issue=2 |pages=271–9 |doi=10.2307/3545638 |jstor=3545638|bibcode=1994Oikos..70..271G }}</ref> and in ponds and potholes.<ref name="vanderValk1989">{{cite book |author=van der Valk, A. G. |title=Northern Prairie Wetlands |date=1989 |publisher=Iowa State University Press |location=Ames, IA}}</ref> Although flooding is the most important factor affecting its distribution, drought, ice scour, grazing, fire and salinity also affect its abundance.<ref name="Keddy">{{cite book |author=Keddy, P.A. |title=Wetland Ecology: Principles and Conservation |date=2010 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |edition=2 |location=Cambridge, UK}}</ref> It can survive unfavourable conditions like prolonged flooding, or drought, as buried seeds.<ref name="vanderValk1976">{{cite journal |author1=van der Valk, A. G. |author2=Davis, C. B. |date=1976 |title=The seed banks of prairie glacial marshes |journal=Canadian Journal of Botany |volume=54 |issue=15 |pages=1832–8 |doi=10.1139/b76-197|bibcode=1976CaJB...54.1832V }}</ref>

==Ecology==
''Scirpus'' species are used as [[Larval food plants of Lepidoptera|food plants]] by the [[larva]]e of some [[Lepidoptera]] species, including ''[[Chedra microstigma]]''<ref name="Busck1914">{{cite journal|last=Busck |first=August |author-link=August Busck |title=New Microlepidoptera from Hawaii |journal=Insecutor Inscitiae Menstruus |date=1914 |volume=2 |issue=7 |page=106 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/9141297}}</ref><ref name="Zimmerman1978">{{cite book |last=Zimmerman |first=Elwood C. |author-link=Elwood Zimmerman |date=1978 |title=Insects of Hawaii |url=https://scholarspace.manoa.hawaii.edu/bitstream/10125/7338/3/IOH-V09%20Microlepidoptera%203of4.pdf |volume='''9''' Microlepidoptera |location=Honolulu |publisher=The University Press of Hawaii |pages=1003–1015}}</ref> and ''[[Scirpophaga nivella]]''.<ref name="Common1960">{{cite journal |last=Common |first=I. F. B. |author-link=:it:Ian Francis Bell Common |date=1960 |title=A revision of the Australian Stem Borers hitherto referred to ''Schoenobius'' and ''Scirpophaga'' (Lepidoptera: Pyralidae, Schoenobiinae) |url=http://www.publish.csiro.au/zo/ZO9600307 |journal=Australian Journal of Zoology |volume=8 |issue=2 |pages=307–347 |doi=10.1071/ZO9600307 |access-date=9 December 2019|url-access=subscription }}</ref> They provide habitat for other wildlife.

Scirpus plants play a vital role in wetland ecosystems by stabilizing soil and reducing erosion. Their dense root systems help filter water and improve its quality.

==Uses==
''Scirpus'' species are often planted to inhibit [[soil erosion]]. They are also used in some [[herbal remedies]]; the plant's [[rhizomes]] are collected in the autumn and winter and dried in the sun before use.
